author: Franktradinglog
text:
The selloff continues. Next, I’m shifting from shorting beta to shorting alpha. I call it the “reverse bottleneck trade”—the counterpart to the earlier bottleneck trade.

The logic is simple: AI demand will keep growing, but that growth may slow, while upstream suppliers keep expanding capacity in response to shortages and fat margins. Once effective supply catches up with demand, bargaining power shifts back downstream. During a shortage, customers care first about availability. Good enough will do. Once supply is plentiful, they start comparing performance, cost, power consumption, and reliability again. That’s when we find out who wins orders on competitiveness and who was simply picking up overflow because the leaders couldn’t supply enough.

My watchlist includes memory runner-up MU, second- and third-tier optical players COHR and AAOI, and foundry runner-up INTC.

This trade doesn’t even require the AI bubble to burst. Supply growth just needs to start outpacing demand growth. I think there’s a very high probability these stocks put in an “Everest chart” over the next year—a towering peak followed by a collapse back down. If you don’t have the stomach to go all-in on outright shorts, anti-bottleneck pair trades are another good way to express the view: long LITE / short AAOI; long TSM / short INTC; long NVDA / short AMD or AVGO.

As I've said before, technological diffusion is an irreversible process, and China has consistently outpaced the US when it comes to driving down costs. The technological moat enjoyed by closed-source frontier AI labs simply cannot last forever.

The latest release of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is yet another reminder of this reality. With only 8B–16B activated parameters, the model reportedly achieved a 77% Pass@1 score on DeepSWE v1.1, outperforming several leading proprietary models on this particular benchmark at a fraction of the cost.

This is a fundamental shift. Open-source models are no longer just "good enough" alternatives to proprietary models. They are increasingly capable of matching—and potentially surpassing—the most advanced closed-source models in specific domains, while dramatically undercutting their economics.

And this process is only accelerating.

Eventually, we'll see highly capable AI models running on a single RTX 5090, or even an ordinary laptop. As intelligence becomes increasingly commoditized and the cost of inference continues to collapse, the scarcity premium embedded in today's AI valuations will become harder and harder to justify.

At that point, continuing to trade the so-called "bottleneck" narrative as if compute scarcity were a permanent structural advantage would be absurd.

The AI trade as we know it is coming to an end.

text:
Thoughts on memory:

Anyone who thinks compute will stay in shortage while memory slides into oversupply must be smoking something. Compute and memory are destined to tighten together or deflate together. One cannot die while the other survives.

By the same logic, the pods shorting memory and going long HDD are out of their minds. How do you think HDD isn't joined at the hip with memory? You really think HDD stays safe if this cycle rolls over?

In the end, all of this comes down to nobody having conviction about what happens after 2027. Historically, we have watched P peak one to two quarters before supply ramps, then Q expands and the entire profit pool collapses. But everyone forgets that this cycle runs on nonstandard products, unlike PCs, smartphones, and general purpose servers, and that it was triggered by factors different from past cycles.

This is because of the boomers who still see memory as an industry where you make a killing in the upcycle and lose your shirt in the downcycle. These self proclaimed veterans view memory through the lens of their past experience, and since they drive the market and set the stock prices, memory trades at such a low valuation. What I keep saying is that a sharp collapse like in the past is impossible. A gradual decline is possible. But even if Samsung and SK Hynix margins were cut in half from current levels, they would still trade at a P/E in the teens. That is still roughly half of HDD valuations.

Personally, I think that as memory prices fall, other sources of demand will absorb the supply at each step down. In particular, I expect personal AI demand, led by local AI, to emerge. Looked at another way, for local AI to take off, the hyperscaler driven spike in memory prices has to be brought under control. At current memory prices, local AI can never diversify.

Just as mainframes gave way to PCs and the cloud gave way to smartphones, each time carrying the cycle from P into a Q expansion phase, I think this AI cycle will also move from frontier labs to local open source AI. Based on these historical precedents, I believe local AI will take over the memory cycle from the frontier labs and carry memory demand.

I am not saying memory prices will hold for more than a decade. Memory P will fall at some point. But what is different from the past is that new consumer devices and new consumer demand, such as open source driven local AI, will support the floor for memory.

So the market right now keeps discounting these stocks out of fear of a memory peak nobody can time. This discount is being driven by boomer investors who dismiss the idea that AI supports the downside and keep pushing the view that earnings will collapse and the trough will revert to past levels too. My point is that this is completely wrong.

DeepSeek is back at it again.

Diving deeper, this happened on a Saturday, no less, so the markets haven't had time to react. Only the weekend perps have.

The headline driving it is DeepSeek's claim that the new model needs 4x less memory per token. 

That reads like less memory demand, until you look at the rest of the release:

+ The model is still huge. It has 552B parameters, and all of them have to sit in memory to run, even though only a fraction is active at a time.

+ It handles 1M tokens of context. Longer context means more memory per user.
+ It's priced at about $1.20 per million output tokens. Cheaper tokens have always meant more tokens used.

+ DeepSeek ran out of compute this week. It had a five-hour outage that experts blamed on not having enough capacity. A company that keeps making its models leaner and still can't keep its service up is evidence that demand is ahead of supply.
